card: Paper card. Question: How can supervised learning strategies combining canonical correlation analysis (CCA) and genetic algorithms (GA) be used to efficiently screen the vast compositional space of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) to identify candidates with high hardness and reasonable ductility?. System: Multi-principal element alloys and high-entropy alloys (HEAs) comprising 5 or more elements; specifically, a 16-element palette (Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, Al, Cu, Mn, Ti, Mo, Nb, Ta, V, W, Zr, Zn, Sn) and synthesized candidates including Co33W07Al33Nb24Cr03 and Ti18Ni24Ta12Cr22Co24.. Processing: Synthesis of candidate alloys via arc-melting compressed pellets of elemental, high-purity powders (Sigma-Aldrich, purity ≥99.9%); pellets were remelted four times to ensure homogeneity; resulting as-cast solid pieces were polished for micro-hardness testing.. Test conditions: Vicker's indentation hardness testing using a LECO LM 248AT model hardness tester with a 100 g load applied for 10 s; at least 20 indents conducted per alloy; ductility assessed via optical microscopic inspection of indentations for cracks.. Findings: A multiple regression analysis of 82 HE alloys yielded a correlation coefficient of 0.79 ± 0.07 between alloy metrics and normalized hardness.; Canonical correlation analysis identified three predictor variables especially relevant to hardness: ΔS′mix (positively correlated), ΔH′mix (negatively correlated), and VEC′ (negatively correlated).; A genetic algorithm (GA) with 1000 generations successfully evolved a population of alloys with fitness values 10–15% greater than the maximum found in the original dataset.; Seven candidate alloys synthesized by arc-melting were tested; five of the seven measured hardnesses fell within the 90% prediction interval of the model.; The highest measured hardness was 1084 ± 37 HV for Co33W07Al33Nb24Cr03.; The second highest measured hardness was 1011 ± 20 HV for Ti18Ni24Ta12Cr22Co24.; All seven synthesized alloys exhibited Pugh ductility ratios (P) less than 0.5, with some showing moderate to considerable ductility (>50% of indentations without cracks).; Microstructural analysis of the hardest alloy (Co33W07Al33Nb24Cr03) revealed a dendritic structure with 13 vol.% inter-dendritic phase, where the hardness was attributed to significant volume fraction of Nb–W solid solution strengthening.. Mechanism: The authors argue that compositional disorder (high ΔS′mix) enhances hardness, while phase separation (high ΔH′mix) and high valence electron concentration (high VEC′) are associated with lower hardness. The high hardness of specific alloys is attributed to solid solution strengthening from significant volume fractions of Nb–W phases, whereas lower hardness in others may result from non-uniform element distribution or the presence of Ta.. Limitations: The authors note that the Pugh criterion is an empirical proxy for ductility and serves as a rough predictor; they also state that further microstructural and computational analysis is needed to confirm the statistical insights regarding the physics of hardness; additionally, the hardest alloy showed some brittleness with cracking near indentation corners.. Future work: The authors propose using the methodology to investigate the impact of processing on property measurements (e.g., mechanical alloying vs. arc-melting), applying the CCA and GA to other properties like yield strength or corrosion resistance, and performing multi-objective Pareto optimization to simultaneously maximize hardness and ductility.. Quote: "We describe here a supervised learning strategy for the efficient screening of HE alloys that combines two complementary tools, namely: (1) a multiple regression analysis and its generalization, a canonical-correlation analysis (CCA) and (2) a genetic algorithm (GA) with a CCA-inspired fitness function."

card: Paper card. Question: Can an entropy-forming-ability (EFA) descriptor based on first-principles energy distribution spectra predict the synthesizability of disordered five-metal refractory carbides as homogeneous high-entropy single phases?. System: Five-metal refractory carbides (MoNbTaVWC5, HfNbTaTiZrC5, HfNbTaTiVC5, HfNbTaTiWC5, NbTaTiVWC5, HfTaTiWZrC5, HfMoTaWZrC5, HfMoTiWZrC5, HfMoVWZrC5) derived from eight metals (Hf, Nb, Mo, Ta, Ti, V, W, Zr) and carbon. Processing: Solid-state synthesis via ball milling (2 h total, 30-min intervals with 10-min rests) followed by Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) at 2200 °C, 100 °C/min heating rate, 30 MPa uniaxial pressure, 5-min dwell in vacuum/argon atmosphere. Test conditions: X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase identification; Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) for chemical homogeneity; Nanoindentation at 27 °C ± 0.5 °C with 50 mN load for Vickers hardness (HV) and elastic modulus (E); Williamson–Hall analysis for lattice strain. Findings: The EFA descriptor correctly predicted that MoNbTaVWC5 (EFA = 125 (eV/atom)−1), HfNbTaTiZrC5 (EFA = 100 (eV/atom)−1), and HfNbTaTiVC5 (EFA = 100 (eV/atom)−1) would form homogeneous single phases, while HfMoVWZrC5 (EFA = 37 (eV/atom)−1) would not.; Six of the nine synthesized compositions (MoNbTaVWC5, HfNbTaTiZrC5, HfNbTaTiVC5, HfNbTaTiWC5, NbTaTiVWC5, HfTaTiWZrC5) exhibited single rock-salt fcc phases, whereas the three lowest-EFA compositions showed multiple secondary phases.; Vickers hardness of HfNbTaTiZrC5 reached 32 GPa, which is 50% higher than the rule of mixtures (ROM) prediction, and HfTaTiWZrC5 reached 33 GPa.; The Pearson correlation between the inverse EFA (EFA−1) and lattice distortion (ε) was 0.97, and the Spearman rank correlation was 0.98, validating EFA as a synthesizability descriptor.; Lattice distortion (ε) ranged from 0.063% for MoNbTaVWC5 (most homogeneous) to 0.325% for HfMoVWZrC5 (least homogeneous).; The highest-EFA composition MoNbTaVWC5 formed a homogeneous phase despite using precursors Mo2C and W2C with different structures (orthorhombic and hexagonal) and stoichiometries compared to the rock-salt product.; Vibrational contributions to formation free energy at 2000 K ranged from ~0 meV/atom to −31 meV/atom, which are significantly smaller than the configurational entropy contributions required to overcome formation enthalpy barriers (50–150 meV/atom).; A threshold of EFA ~50 (eV/atom)−1 was identified as the point above which homogeneous disordered single phases are likely to form.. Mechanism: The authors argue that a narrow energy distribution spectrum (low standard deviation σ) implies a low energy cost to access metastable configurations, promoting configurational randomness (entropy) at finite temperatures. This entropy stabilization allows the disordered rock-salt phase to remain locked in upon cooling, even when competing ordered phases exist. Enhanced hardness is attributed to mass disorder causing impedance mismatch that scatters dislocations, increasing resistance to plastic deformation.. Limitations: The study notes that the Williamson–Hall formalism does not provide particularly accurate absolute values of lattice strain (ε), though it is effective for relative comparisons. Additionally, the vibrational contribution to entropy is an order of magnitude smaller than configurational entropy, and the study did not investigate the specific effect of carbon stoichiometry on melting points.. Future work: The authors state that an investigation of the effect of carbon stoichiometry is clearly warranted to understand how vacancies might further improve high-temperature performance, although it is outside the scope of this study.. Quote: "The descriptor correctly predicts the ease with which compositions can be experimentally synthesized as rock-salt high-entropy homogeneous phases, validating the ansatz, and in some cases, going beyond intuition."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the number of principal elements (N) in equimolar multi-principal element alloys affect the probability of forming disordered solid solution (SS) phases versus intermetallic (IM) phases, and what are the implications for high-temperature structural applications?. System: Equimolar combinations of 3 to 6 elements from a palette of 26 metallic elements (including Al, Si, Mo, Ta, W, Nb, Ti, V, Re, Zr, Cr, Fe, Co, Ni, etc.). Processing: High-throughput computational screening using the CALPHAD method (Pandat v.8.1 software) to calculate phase diagrams for 134,547 equimolar alloy systems; results filtered for credibility where the fraction of fully assessed binary systems (fAB) equals 1.. Test conditions: Phase diagrams calculated between 600 °C and 3,600 °C; properties evaluated at the solidus temperature (Tm) and at 600 °C; maximum use temperature (Tuse) estimated as the lowest of 0.8Tm or the last first-order phase reaction temperature below Tm.. Findings: The fraction of solid solution (SS) alloys decreases as the number of elements (N) increases: at Tm, 30% of 3-component alloys are SS, dropping to only 5% for 6-component alloys.; Configurational entropy rises slowly with N (as ln(N)), while the number of binary interactions increases rapidly (as (N/2)(N−1)), explaining why IM formation becomes more probable as N increases.; The maximum solidus temperature (Tm) decreases with N: 2,925 °C for 3-component, 2,754 °C for 4-component, 2,435 °C for 5-component, and 2,056 °C for 6-component alloys.; The maximum maximum use temperature (Tuse) decreases with N: 2,285 °C for 3-component, 1,846 °C for 4-component, 1,677 °C for 5-component, and 1,159 °C for 6-component alloys.; Only 3 out of 209 SS alloys with Tuse ≥ 1,000 °C are 6-component alloys, whereas 108 are 3-component alloys.; Extreme property values (highest/lowest density, modulus, cost) are achieved in ternary (3-component) alloys, while 6-component alloys show tighter property spreads.; 51 equimolar alloy systems with 3 ≤ N ≤ 5 were identified that satisfy aggressive design criteria (Tuse ≥ 1,000 °C, density ≤ 10 g cm−3, modulus ≥ 100 GPa, cost ≤ $200/kg, no IM phases at Tm).. Mechanism: The authors argue that while configurational entropy (Smix) favors solid solution stability, it increases only logarithmically with the number of elements. Conversely, the number of binary element pairs increases quadratically, raising the probability that at least one pair has a sufficiently large negative formation enthalpy (Hf) to overcome the entropy term in the Gibbs free energy equation (G = H - TS), thereby stabilizing intermetallic phases.. Limitations: The study is restricted to equimolar compositions; non-equimolar alloys were not explored and may offer higher Tm or Tuse values. Additionally, the credibility filter (fAB=1) excluded over 95% of the calculated systems, potentially missing viable alloys if less stringent criteria were acceptable.. Future work: The authors propose extending the screening to non-equimolar alloys to uncover local compositions with extreme properties, conducting more extensive experimental validations to potentially relax credibility criteria, and developing high-throughput experimental techniques capable of handling microstructural length scales.. Quote: "We find the surprising result that solid solution alloys become less likely as the number of alloy elements increases."

card: Paper card. Question: What thermodynamic factors and specific elemental additions dictate the occurrence of liquid phase separation (LPS) versus single-phase solidification in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), and how do these factors influence microstructure formation?. System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs), multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs), and complex concentrated alloys (CCAs), specifically systems containing Co, Cr, Cu, Fe, Ni, Mn, Al, Ti, V, Nb, Ag, Sn, Mo, and Y2O3 (e.g., CoCrCuFeNi, AgAlCoCrCuNi, CoCrCu, CoCrCuNi, CoCrCuFeNi, CoCrCuMnNi, CoCrCuNiV, AlCoCrCuFeNiSi0.5). Processing: Arc-melting, induction melting, laser cladding, electromagnetic levitation, rapid solidification, and undercooling experiments (e.g., drop tube, molten fused silica fluxing); specific undercooling temperatures noted include ~150 K, 160 K, 190 K, 293 K, and 381 K (0.23Tm). Test conditions: Solidification from liquid state under varying cooling rates (slow cooling, rapid solidification), undercooling past critical temperatures (ΔTcrit), and in-situ neutron transmission imaging during heating and cooling of CoCrCu alloys. Findings: Positive mixing enthalpy (ΔHmix) not compensated by entropy of mixing leads to liquid phase separation.; Co, Ni, and Ti promote miscibility in HEAs/CCAs/MPEAs, while Cr, V, and Nb raise the miscibility gap temperature and increase LPS.; Addition of appropriate amounts of Ni to equiatomic CoCrCu eliminates immiscibility, allowing CoCrCuNi, CoCrCuFeNi, and CoCrCuMnNi to solidify dendritically.; Only three out of ten tested additions to equiatomic CoCrCu (Ni, Fe, Mn) resulted in dendritic solidification; the rest underwent stable LPS.; In CoCrCuFeNi, metastable LPS occurs when undercooling exceeds ΔTcrit values of 100 K (Guo et al.), 160 K (x=1.0), 190 K (x=1.5), and 293 K (x=2.0).; In AgAlCoCrCuNi, the addition of Ag caused phase separation into Cu-rich globules embedded in Cu-depleted phases.; The addition of 1 wt.% nanosized Y2O3 to AlCoCrCuFeNiSi0.5 caused liquids to separate into egg-like globules of Cu-rich liquids inside Cu-depleted liquid.; LPS in CoCrCuFeNi significantly decreases yield strength and elongation due to microstructure non-uniformity.. Mechanism: Liquid phase separation is driven by positive deviations from Raoult's law and positive enthalpy of mixing (ΔHmix > 0), which creates a preference for nearest neighbors of similar atoms. When the enthalpy term (ΔHmix) exceeds the entropy term (TΔS) in the Gibbs free energy equation, the system decomposes into two immiscible liquids (L1 + L2). In metastable cases, undercooling allows the alloy to enter a miscibility gap beneath the liquidus curve that is not present in equilibrium conditions. Constitutional LPS occurs when compositional changes in the interdendritic liquid during solidification trigger separation.. Limitations: The text notes that it is impossible to visualize the phase diagram space of multicomponent alloy systems containing 5+ elements, making it difficult to predict liquid phase separation without computational screening. Additionally, the lack of experimental data for mixing enthalpies of many binary alloys necessitates the use of models like Miedema's for approximations.. Future work: The authors suggest the need for creative ideas to understand the nature of solidification in multicomponent alloys due to the impossibility of orthogonal element phase diagram visualization. They also highlight the need to amend ΔHmix criteria for predicting single-phase formation to include the possibility of liquid phase separation when ΔHmix > 0.. Quote: "Positive mixing enthalpy if not compensated by the entropy of mixing will lead to liquid phase separation."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the addition of Ni to the immiscible equiatomic CoCrCu system affect liquid state miscibility and solidification behavior, and can in-situ neutron imaging capture this remixing process?. System: Equiatomic CoCrCu buttons with added elemental Ni buttons to form equiatomic CoCrCuNi (CoCrCu + Ni). Processing: Arc-melted CoCrCu buttons and remelted Ni buttons placed in an alumina crucible inside a high-temperature vacuum furnace (HOT-A furnace) at ≈1 × 10−6 mbar; heated to 1500 °C, held for 150 radiographs (approx. 35 min), then cooled to 1000 °C. Test conditions: In-situ neutron imaging at CG-1D Neutron Imaging Instrument using cold neutrons (0.8 < λ < 6 Å); 10 radiographs acquired every 20 °C from 1000 °C to 1500 °C and back to 1000 °C; ramp rate 20 °C/min; acquisition time 10 s/radiograph; spatial resolution ~200 μm. Findings: Onset of melting observed at approximately 1100 °C, with complete dissolution of phases at ~1420 °C.; Solidification of the CoCrCuNi alloy initiates at ~1320 °C.; No changes in neutron attenuation were observed during the solidification of the CoCrCuNi alloy, indicating solidification from a single-phase liquid.; Thermodynamic calculations indicate the CoCrCuNix alloy solidifies from a single-phase liquid when x ≥ 0.275, close to the nominal concentration of x = 0.25.; The CT images of the solidified CoCrCuNi alloy show uniform contrast with no macroscopic-phase separations, unlike the heterogeneous CoCrCu alloy.; The miscibility gap in the CoCrCu system is eliminated by the addition of Ni, allowing the Cu-rich liquid to enter the solution.; The furnace thermocouple temperature is estimated to be about 15 °C higher than the sample during heating.. Mechanism: Ni acts as a solubility pathway for the Cu-rich liquid phase to enter the solution with the overall melt, transforming the previously immiscible CoCr-rich and Cu-rich liquids into a single-phase liquid upon dissolution.. Limitations: The accuracy of the temperature measurements is within ±15 °C due to the difference between furnace thermocouple readings and actual sample temperature.. Future work: The authors propose that in-situ neutron imaging of solidification can provide a novel solution to probe the liquid phases of calculated isopleths and provide valuable insight into the liquid state behavior of HEAs.. Quote: "The neutron imaging shows that the solidification of CoCrCuNi results from a single-phase liquid."

card: Paper card. Question: Is it feasible to produce the refractory metal high entropy alloy W20Mo20Ta20Nb20V20 via in-situ alloy formation using laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M) from elemental powders, and how do process parameters influence defect formation, microstructure, and phase composition?. System: W20Mo20Ta20Nb20V20 (refractory metal high entropy alloy) fabricated from a heterogeneous mixture of elemental W, Mo, Ta, Nb, and V powders.. Processing: Laser Powder Bed Fusion (PBF-LB/M) using an AconityMINI machine with a 1 kW fiber laser (1080 nm) on a Mo substrate in Argon atmosphere (<25 ppm O2). Two parameter sets were used: Set A (600 W, 800 mm/s, 120 µm hatch, 125 J/mm³) and Set B (100 W, 100 mm/s, 45 µm hatch, 889 J/mm³). Vanadium powder content was increased by a factor of 1.5 to compensate for evaporation.. Test conditions: Samples (6 × 6 × 6 mm³) were analyzed via optical microscopy, SEM, EBSD, TEM, and microhardness testing. Microhardness was measured as HV0.1. Cooling rates are estimated at 10⁶ K/s.. Findings: Relative densities reached 99.8% for parameter set A and 99.5% for parameter set B.; A single bcc-phase was confirmed by EBSD and TEM, consistent with vacuum arc melted samples.; Average grain size was 16.3 µm for PBF-LB/M B, which is more than four times smaller than the 80 µm reported for vacuum arc melted samples.; Parameter set B (higher volumetric energy density) resulted in fewer undissolved tungsten particles compared to set A.; Parameter set A exhibited smaller cracks than set B, which showed wider cracks due to higher internal stress.; Microhardness of the coarser structure (Set A) was 561 ± 17 HV0.1, while the finer cellular structure (Set B) was 614 ± 21 HV0.1.; Elemental segregation was observed: V concentrated in interdendritic areas, while W and Ta were predominantly in intradendritic areas.; Solidification mode shifted from dendritic (Set A) to cellular (Set B) based on growth rate (R) and temperature gradient (G) conditions.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the formation of undissolved W particles to the high melting point of tungsten, which requires high volumetric energy input and slow scan speeds to dissolve. Cracking is caused by internal stresses from the PBF-LB/M process combined with the alloy's low room temperature ductility and brittle grain boundaries (likely due to O and N impurities). The microstructure (dendritic vs. cellular) is controlled by the ratio of growth rate (R) to temperature gradient (G), where higher R and lower G favor dendrites, while lower R and higher G favor cellular structures.. Limitations: Samples contained cracks and undissolved tungsten particles; completely defect-free samples were not produced. The study notes that the alloy has limited room temperature ductility and fracture toughness.. Future work: The authors suggest using a high-temperature (>600 °C) build-platform heating device and/or high-purity powder with low O and N content to achieve crack-free processing. They also propose verifying if more recently developed refractory metal high entropy alloys with increased room temperature ductility can be processed without high-temperature heating.. Quote: "The relative density of the samples with a dimension of 6 × 6 × 6 mm3 reaches, in dependence of the PBF-LB/M parameter set, 99.8%."

card: Paper card. Question: How can the room temperature ductility of an initially brittle refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) with a continuous ordered B2 matrix be improved while maintaining high yield strength?. System: Al0.5NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr (Refractory High Entropy Alloy). Processing: 1. Vacuum/argon arc melting followed by hot isostatic pressing (HIP) at 1200 °C for 2 hours under 210 MPa argon. 2. Homogenization at 1200 °C for 24 hours followed by slow cooling (10 °C/min) to room temperature (Condition 1). 3. Solutionizing Condition 1 at 1400 °C for 20 min followed by water quenching (Condition 2). 4. Annealing Condition 2 at 600 °C for 120 hrs followed by water quenching (Condition 3).. Test conditions: Room temperature (RT) and 600 °C uniaxial compression testing at a strain rate of 0.001 s−1; Vickers microhardness (4.9 N load, 15 s dwell); Microstructural characterization via SEM, TEM, and Atom Probe Tomography (APT).. Findings: Condition (1) (continuous B2 matrix) exhibited a yield strength of 2035 MPa but only 4.5% compressive strain before fracture.; Condition (2) (single-phase weakly ordered BCC) showed high ductility with no fracture after 60% true strain but lower yield strength (1065 MPa).; Condition (3) (inverted microstructure with discrete B2 precipitates in continuous BCC matrix) achieved a yield strength of 1345 MPa and 16.9% peak strain with fracture at 38% strain.; At 600 °C, Condition (3) showed anomalous strengthening with a yield strength of 1423 MPa (higher than its RT value of 1345 MPa) and 16.2% plasticity.; APT analysis revealed strong elemental partitioning: B2 phase is rich in Al and Zr, while BCC phase is rich in Nb and Ta.; The microstructure of Condition (3) consists of discrete B2 precipitates (~50 nm) within a continuous disordered BCC matrix, contrasting with Condition (1) where B2 is the continuous matrix.; Condition (1) hardness was 562 ± 16 HV, Condition (2) was 405 ± 11 HV, and Condition (3) was 475 ± 12 HV.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the poor ductility in Condition (1) is caused by the continuous ordered B2 matrix, which is inherently brittle. The improved ductility in Condition (3) is attributed to the 'inversion' of the microstructure, where the continuous phase becomes the more ductile disordered BCC matrix, while the hard B2 phase exists as discrete precipitates providing strengthening. The anomalous strengthening at 600 °C in Condition (3) is speculated to result from competing slip systems in the complex B2 phase (e.g., <001>{110} and <111>{112}) leading to sessile kinks or dislocation debris, similar to mechanisms in Ni3Al.. Limitations: The authors state that the details of the strengthening mechanisms are beyond the scope of the study and that the explanation for the anomalous strengthening at 600 °C is highly speculative. They note that applying classical precipitation hardening models requires parameters (lattice misfit, elastic properties, fault energies) that are difficult to quantify in this complex RHEA.. Future work: The authors recommend additional scientific studies to establish the influence of concentrated alloy additions on precipitation strengthening parameters, further investigation of deformation mechanisms at room temperature and 600 °C, and additional studies at higher temperatures and under tensile loading.. card: Paper card. Question: Can a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy be successfully fabricated via selective laser melting (SLM) despite the high melting points of its constituent elements, and what are the resulting microstructural, mechanical, and corrosion properties compared to traditional superalloys?. System: NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (nominal equiatomic composition: Nb 99.9%, Mo 99.9%, Ta 99.9%, W 99.9%). Processing: Selective Laser Melting (SLM) using FORWEDO LM120 equipment with a 500 W fiber laser in an argon atmosphere (<20 ppm oxygen); initial parameters: hatch distance 0.1 mm, layer thickness 0.1 mm, laser power factor 0.8, scanning velocity 250 mm/s, S-cross scanning; followed by a remelting process (3 total passes per layer) to achieve a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. Test conditions: Microstructure and composition analyzed via SEM (HITACHI SU-8010) and EDS; crystal structure via XRD (Cu target, λ = 1.54 Å); microhardness measured on XY plane; corrosion resistance tested via potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution (scanning voltage −0.2 V to +0.2 V) and high-voltage scanning (−1.5 to +2 V). Findings: A single BCC solid solution was formed without secondary phases, with an experimental lattice parameter of 3.2034 Å.; Elements with lower melting points and densities (Nb and Mo) showed negative molar ratio deviations of up to 3.5% (Nb: −3.5 at%, Mo: −0.16 at%) compared to the nominal 25%.; The average grain size was 13.4 μm, significantly smaller than the 200 μm observed in as-cast NbMoTaW HEA.; Primary and secondary dendrite arm spacings were 6.59 μm and 1.68 μm, respectively, much finer than the 20–30 μm spacing in as-cast samples.; The average microhardness of the SLM-fabricated sample reached 826 Hv, compared to 446 Hv for arc-melted HEA and 310–437 Hv for superalloys.; The free-corrosion current (Icorr) of the NbMoTaW HEA was 8.716 × 10−11 A, which is two orders of magnitude lower than that of 316 L steel (8.815 × 10−9 A).; Visual corrosion testing showed 316 L steel suffered up to 1 mm corrosion depth, while the NbMoTaW alloy exhibited only crack extension and minor pitting.. Mechanism: The rapid solidification in SLM creates extremely high temperature gradients and cooling rates, limiting growth time and resulting in fine grains and slender dendrites. Composition deviations occur because powders with lower melting points and densities fuse first, spread over larger areas, absorb more energy, and evaporate earlier during the process. The improved hardness is attributed to grain refinement following the Hall–Petch law, while superior corrosion resistance is due to the presence of easily passivating elements (Nb, Mo, Ta) despite minor segregation.. Limitations: The ductility of the NbMoTaW HEA at room temperature remains low, and while composition deviation exists (up to 3.5%), it is noted that further study of mechanical properties is still necessary.. Future work: Further study of mechanical properties is required to fully assess the potential of the SLM-fabricated NbMoTaW HEA.. Quote: "The HEA shows an excellent microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance performance compared with traditional superalloys."

card: Paper card. Question: How does varying tungsten concentration affect the crystal structure, microstructure, and mechanical properties (hardness, strength, ductility) of WxNbMoTa refractory high-entropy alloys fabricated via laser cladding deposition?. System: WxNbMoTa refractory high-entropy alloys with x = 0, 0.16, 0.33, 0.53 (mole fractions). Processing: Laser cladding deposition (LCD) using a coaxial LCD system with 565 W laser power, 8 mm/s scanning speed, 0.08 mm layer thickness, and 600 °C induction heating temperature; powders (45–125 μm) mixed for 4 h and dried at 120 °C for 8 h in Argon (<80 ppm O2). Test conditions: Vickers microhardness (500 g load, 30 s); room temperature compression (25 °C, 0.001 s⁻¹); high-temperature compression (1000 °C, 3.5 min heating, 15 min soak, 0.001 s⁻¹ strain rate, 10⁻³ torr vacuum). Findings: All WxNbMoTa alloys formed a single-phase body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution regardless of tungsten content.; Grain and dendrite sizes averaged 20 μm and 4 μm, respectively, due to rapid solidification in LCD.; Vickers microhardness increased with tungsten concentration: 459.2 ± 9.7, 476.0 ± 12.9, 485.3 ± 8.7, and 497.6 ± 5.6 Hv for x = 0, 0.16, 0.33, 0.53.; NbMoTa (x = 0) exhibited yield strength of 530 MPa and compressive strain of 8.5% at 1000 °C.; At room temperature, NbMoTa showed yield strength of 874 MPa and compressive strain of 5.8%, while W-containing alloys were brittle with compressive strengths of 840–895 MPa.; Bulk modulus increased with tungsten content: 174, 182, 186, and 192 GPa for x = 0, 0.16, 0.33, 0.53.; Spherical gas porosities in as-fabricated samples were eliminated by using molybdenum powders with higher granule density and good sphericity.. Mechanism: Rapid solidification during laser cladding deposition (melting in 10⁻³–10⁻² s) suppresses constitutional segregation and promotes fine equiaxed grains. Tungsten addition increases lattice distortion and solid solution strengthening, raising hardness and bulk modulus but reducing ductility at room temperature. Porosity formation is attributed to adsorbed Argon gas in low-density molybdenum powder particles, not microstructure features.. Limitations: Spherical gas porosities appeared in samples fabricated with standard molybdenum powders due to low granule density; tungsten addition reduces room-temperature plasticity, making W-containing alloys brittle.. Future work: The present work provides a theoretical basis for LCD manufacturing of aerospace parts of refractory HEAs with large size, complex structure, and variable composition.. Quote: "The size of the grains and dendrites are 20 μm and 4 μm on average, due to the rapid solidification characteristics of the laser cladding deposition."

card: Paper card. Question: How can high-entropy alloys be recommended effectively when existing data is limited, biased, and lacks sufficient descriptors for alloys with varying numbers of components?. System: Equiatomic alloys comprising elements from the set {Fe, Co, Ir, Cu, Ni, Pt, Pd, Rh, Au, Ag, Ru, Os, Si, As, Al, Tc, Re, Mn, Ta, Ti, W, Mo, Cr, V, Hf, Nb, Zr}, specifically focusing on Fe-Co-based quaternary alloys (FeMnCoNi) and early transition metal alloys.. Processing: Development of an evidence-based recommender system (ERS) using Dempster–Shafer theory to model, collect, and combine pieces of evidence from existing datasets without using material descriptors; experimental validation involved synthesizing Fe0.25Co0.25Mn0.25Ni0.25 thin films annealed at 400 °C.. Test conditions: Evaluation performed via k-fold cross-validation on four datasets (ASMI16, CALPHAD, AFLOW, LTVC) containing binary, ternary, quaternary, and quinary alloys; extrapolation tests conducted on quaternary and quinary HEAs; experimental validation on thin films annealed at 400 °C.. Findings: The ERS outperforms matrix-factorization (NMF, SVD) and supervised-learning (SVM, logistic regression, decision tree, naive Bayes) systems in k-fold cross-validation across all four datasets.; The ERS demonstrates superior extrapolation capabilities, requiring approximately 10–100 fewer trials to recall 50% and 75% of quinary HEAs compared to NMF and SVD systems.; Supervised-learning methods failed to rank HEAs effectively in datasets containing only positively labeled HEAs, performing either randomly or failing to rank any.; The ERS identified FeCoMnNi as the only Fe-Mn-Co-based quaternary candidate with a belief higher than 0.5.; Experimental validation confirmed that the Fe0.25Co0.25Mn0.25Ni0.25 thin film annealed at 400 °C exhibits a body-centered cubic (BCC) structure, evidenced by a reflection at 2θ = 44.7°.; Similarity analysis revealed three distinct element groups corresponding to early transition metals, late transition metals, and a third group with no evidence of similarity in the ASMI16 dataset.; Elements with the same periodic table group index (Δgroup = 0) showed high similarity scores, while similarity decreased as Δgroup increased to 3 or 4.; In the absence of sufficient evidence for mixtures of many elements, the system retained a large degree of uncertainty, with m({HEA, ¬HEA}) ≈ 1.. Mechanism: The ERS uses the elemental substitution method where pairs of observed alloys serve as evidence to measure substitutability between element combinations; Dempster–Shafer theory assigns mass functions to subsets of a frame of discernment ({similar, dissimilar} or {HEA, ¬HEA}) to model uncertainty, combining multiple pieces of evidence using the Dempster rule to rank potential alloys without relying on material descriptors.. Limitations: The system does not answer essential questions regarding the specific crystal structure or other properties of the HEAs beyond phase existence; detailed quantitative investigation of secondary phases in the synthesized FeCoMnNi alloy thin film was not done due to technical difficulties; the system cannot reliably recall the remaining one-quarter of HEAs in some datasets due to insufficient evidence in the training data.. Future work: The authors propose that by redesigning the frame of discernment to reflect additional properties of interest, the model can be constructed to recommend potential alloys forming HEA phases with desirable properties beyond just phase existence.. Quote: "To overcome these issues, here we show the development of an evidence-based material recommender system (ERS) that adopts Dempster–Shafer theory, a general framework for reasoning with uncertainty."

Paper card. Question: How can a recommender system be constructed to identify unknown High-Entropy Alloy (HEA) compositions and extrapolate recommendations to higher-order alloys (quaternary and quinary) based on binary and ternary training data?. System: Alloys composed of 27 elements; specific datasets include D_AFLOW (binary/ternary), D_LTVC (binary/ternary), D_ASMI16 (binary), D_CALPHAD (ternary); case study: Fe0.25Co0.25Mn0.25Ni0.25 thin films. Processing: Machine learning: Grid search for hyperparameter α (0.01 to 0.9); Ninefold cross-validation repeated 100 times; Experimental: Combinatorial multitarget radio frequency sputtering (100 W FeCoMn, 120 W Ni) at 0.3 Pa Ar, deposition rate 0.23 ± 0.01 nm s–1, annealing at 400 °C for 30 min under vacuum < 6 × 10−3 Pa. Test conditions: Cross-validation on D_AFLOW (80% accuracy), D_LTVC (75% accuracy), D_ASMI16 (40/45 training, 5/45 test), D_CALPHAD (216/243 training, 27/243 test); Extrapolation to 17,550 quaternary and 80,730 quinary alloys; Thin film characterization via XRD and XRF. Findings: Cross-validated testing accuracy rates were 80% for D_AFLOW and 75% for D_LTVC.; The absolute value of alpha (α) has little effect on the final result of the recommender system.; A total of 351 hypothetical binary alloys were generated from 27 elements, with 45 in the training set and 306 ranked by the model.; For ternary alloys, 2,925 hypothetical combinations were generated from 27 elements, with 243 in the training set and 2,682 ranked.; The model ranked 17,550 quaternary alloys and 80,730 quinary alloys for synthesis candidates.; The BCC phase was confirmed for the annealed thin film sample at the equiatomic composition of FeCoMnNi.; Phase separation and inflection points were observed near 400 °C for FeCoMn-X compositions.. Mechanism: The system uses a rating matrix representation where alloys are decomposed into elementary components (A and B) to build a user-item matrix. It learns a similarity matrix between elements (and binary combinations) from training data to predict ratings for missing elements, allowing the ranking of hypothetical alloys. The method accounts for uncertainty by adding a degree of uncertainty α in the mass function.. Limitations: The compositional descriptor cannot be applied in the case of having extrapolation in the number of components. The experiments do not use the selected alloys (test set) to improve the accuracy of the model for the next trial due to computational cost.. Future work: Structural changes at higher temperatures for FeCoMnNi are expected and are currently under investigation.. Quote: "The compositional descriptor therefore cannot be applied in the case of having extrapolation in the number of components."

card: Paper card. Question: Can a novel material descriptor based on valence shell electron distribution and local coordination effectively predict local magnetic moments, formation energies, and atomization energies while providing interpretability in terms of physical chemistry?. System: Bimetal alloys of lanthanide metal and transition-metal (LAT) including Mn, Fe, Co, Ni; LATX alloys (X = B, C, N, O); transition-metal binary alloys (TT); organic molecules from the QM7 dataset. Processing: Computed local magnetic moments using VASP 5.4.1 with GGA/PBE functional, 520 eV energy cutoff, 150 k-point mesh density, and 0.1eV Gaussian smearing; constructed Orbital-Field Matrix (OFM) descriptors using Voronoi polyhedra for coordination numbers and inverse distance weighting; performed decision tree regression and Kernel Ridge Regression (KRR) with Laplacian kernel. Test conditions: Cross-validated on 658 LAT structures for magnetic moments; 4000+ crystalline compounds (LATX, TTX, LAT, TT) for formation energies; 6915 organic molecules (QM7) for atomization energies. Findings: OFM achieved a cross-validated RMSE of 0.19 eV/atom and R² of 0.98 for formation energies of crystalline systems, outperforming the Coulomb Matrix (CM) descriptor (RMSE 0.47 eV/atom, R² 0.87).; For local magnetic moments in LAT alloys, KRR using OFM yielded an RMSE of 0.13 μB and R² of 0.93, slightly better than the CM descriptor (RMSE 0.15 μB, R² 0.90).; Decision tree analysis revealed that the magnetic moment of Fe sites is less than 2.0 μB when the coordination number of occupied d orbitals is less than 6.6 or greater than 9.15.; For Ni sites, a large magnetic moment (> 1.0 μB) is obtained when the coordination number of occupied d orbitals is greater than 8.25.; The OFM descriptor for the QM7 organic molecules dataset required only 25 non-zero features despite high dimensionality, whereas LATX datasets exhibited a large variety of OFMs.; The OFM achieved a cross-validated RMSE of 0.043 eV/atom and R² of 0.98 for atomization energies of organic molecules, comparable to the CM descriptor (RMSE 0.040 eV/atom, R² 0.99).; The OFM demonstrated superior prediction ability for LATX systems with high diversity in atomic composition and structure compared to the CM approach.. Mechanism: The OFM encodes the coordination of valence electrons and the number of orbitals j coordinating the center orbital i, incorporating distance-dependent weights via inverse distance. This representation captures the ligand field and crystal field effects, where the coordination numbers of occupied d orbitals of transition-metals and occupied f orbitals of lanthanides determine local magnetic moments through T-T and LA-T exchange interactions.. Limitations: The OFM includes the effect of nearest neighbor sites chosen by Voronoi polyhedra only, potentially missing long-range interactions that the CM descriptor captures via power-law decay; for simple organic molecules (QM7), the CM descriptor yields slightly better results than OFM.. Future work: The authors suggest that OFM could be useful for mining chemical/physical information on materials from available datasets using modern machine learning algorithms and for the theoretical design of materials properties via an approach similar to building blocks.. Quote: "We propose a novel representation of materials named an 'orbital-field matrix (OFM)', which is based on the distribution of valence shell electrons."

card: Paper card. Question: How can a data-driven protocol be established to measure the similarity between materials based on specific physical properties to uncover underlying mechanisms and improve property prediction?. System: Three datasets: (1) 239 binary AB materials with Fm-3m (NaCl) structure; (2) 1541 binary AB body-centred cubic (b.c.c.) crystals; (3) 101 binary rare earth–transition metal alloys.. Processing: Three-step protocol: (i) Kernel ridge regression (GKR) with exhaustive search of all variable combinations (e.g., 2^17-1 = 131,071 combinations) and 3x10-fold cross-validation to select combinations with R^2 > 0.90; (ii) Regression-based clustering using sparse linear regression (L1 regularization) and K-means modifications to partition data into k clusters; (iii) Construction of a committee machine from clustering results to generate an affinity matrix for hierarchical clustering.. Test conditions: Experiment 1: Formation energy (E_form) prediction; Experiment 2: Lattice constant (L_const) prediction; Experiment 3: Curie temperature (T_C) prediction. Calculations performed on a high-performance cluster (256 cores, 1.1 TB RAM).. Findings: In Experiment 1, the R^2 score for formation energy prediction improved from 0.972 (MAE: 0.117 eV) to 0.982 (MAE: 0.101 eV) by using similarity-based regression.; In Experiment 2, the R^2 score for lattice constant prediction improved marginally from 0.991 (MAE: 0.013 Å) to 0.992 (MAE: 0.011 Å).; In Experiment 3, the R^2 score for Curie temperature prediction improved significantly from 0.974 (MAE: 37.87 K) to 0.991 (MAE: 24.16 K).; The method identified distinct material groups: G1 (oxides, nitrides, carbides with specific oxidation states) and G2 (halides, oxides, etc.) in the Fm-3m dataset.; For b.c.c. crystals, three groups were identified: G1 (heavy transition metals), G2 (metal and non-metal), and G3 (metal and non-metal with different lattice constant dependencies).; For rare earth–transition metal alloys, G1 included high T_C Mn- and Co-based alloys, while G2 included Fe-based Fe17RE2 alloys.; The affinity matrix values ranged from 0 (never in same cluster) to 1 (always in same cluster), with intra-group affinities exceeding 0.7 and inter-group affinities below 0.2 in Experiment 1.. Mechanism: The authors argue that materials belonging to the same cluster in the regression-based models share the same 'actuating mechanisms' for the target physical property. By constructing a committee machine that votes on cluster membership across multiple high-accuracy regression models, the method captures multilateral similarities that reflect the underlying physics, allowing for more accurate local linear modeling when predicting properties for new materials.. Limitations: The exhaustive search for variable selection based on kernel regression consumes significant computing resources (e.g., 36, 41, and 28 hours for the three experiments) due to combinatorial explosion. Additionally, no significant improvement in R^2 was observed for the lattice constant prediction problem compared to the other two properties.. Future work: The text states the method can 'systematically facilitate further understanding of a given phenomenon by identifying similarities among materials' and implies future application to other properties, but does not explicitly list specific future work projects beyond the general utility of the protocol.. Quote: "The method consists of three steps: variable evaluation based on nonlinear regression, regression-based clustering, and similarity measurement with a committee machine constructed from the clustering results."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the addition of scandium (Sc) to the equimolar Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr refractory high-entropy alloy system affect its crystal structure, microstructure, and superconducting properties?. System: Equimolar Sc-Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr refractory high-entropy alloys (nine alloys: five 4-component, three 5-component, one 6-component). Processing: Arc melting in an Ar atmosphere; ingots remelted several times and cooled naturally to as-cast state. Test conditions: Electrical resistivity (0.35–300 K, 0–9 T), specific heat (0.35–8.5 K, 0–9 T), magnetic susceptibility (1.8–400 K, up to 7 T), XRD, SEM BSE, EDS. Findings: Addition of Sc transforms the single-phase bcc structure of the parent Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr system into a two-phase structure containing bcc and hexagonal close-packed (hcp) phases.; The hcp phase absorbs practically all Sc, while the bcc phase remains Sc-poor and identical to the parent system's bcc phase.; Microstructure becomes highly inhomogeneous with large bcc dendrites (10–100 µm) that are homogeneous in the center but show a fine dispersion of sub-micron precipitates at the edges.; Interdendritic regions consist of a fine dispersion of bcc and hcp precipitates (10–100 nm) with hcp precipitates in the majority.; Superconducting transition temperatures (TCρ) range from 6.4 K to 8.4 K across the alloys.; The superconducting molar fraction (x) at T→0 ranges from 61% to 86%, correlating linearly with the bcc phase fraction.; The Sc-containing hcp phase fraction is non-superconducting, while the Sc-poor bcc phase fraction exhibits superconducting parameters identical to the parent Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys.; The superconducting phase is classified as a type II, BCS-like, 'dirty' superconductor.. Mechanism: Scandium has strong repulsion to Nb and Ta (positive binary mixing enthalpies) and affinity for Zr, driving phase separation into Sc-poor bcc and Sc-rich hcp phases. The hcp phase is non-superconducting due to the presence of Sc, while the bcc phase retains the superconductivity of the parent system. The inhomogeneous microstructure arises from the clustering of elements with similar atomic radii and the phase separation driven by mixing enthalpies.. Limitations: The authors state that mechanical properties and corrosion resistance were deferred to another study. Additionally, accurate chemical composition of the dark (hcp) phase could not be determined in interdendritic regions due to the fine dispersion of precipitates preventing reliable EDS analysis of individual phases.. Future work: The authors propose that the mechanical properties and corrosion resistance of the Sc-Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys will be investigated in a separate study.. Quote: "The addition of Sc produces a two-phase structure in the Sc-Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys, with one phase being bcc and the other hexagonal close-packed (hcp)."
W4210276750.title: The Effect of Scandium on the Structure, Microstructure and Superconductivity of Equimolar Sc-Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr Refractory High-Entropy Alloys

card: Paper card. Question: How does the addition of scandium (0.3–5 wt.%) affect the microstructure, phase stability, mechanical properties, and thermoelectric performance of Al-containing high-entropy alloys (Al2CoCrFeNi, Al0.5CoCrCuFeNi, and AlCoCrCu0.5FeNi)?. System: Al2CoCrFeNi, Al0.5CoCrCuFeNi, and AlCoCrCu0.5FeNi high-entropy alloys alloyed with 0.3–5 wt.% Sc. Processing: Induction melting of pure metallic powders in a BN crucible under Ar atmosphere at >1300 °C for 5 min, re-melted three times; annealing at 850–930 °C for 6–12 h in sealed silica tubes under vacuum (<10−7 Pa) followed by quenching in ice-cold water. Test conditions: Vickers hardness (9.81 N load); small punch tests; DSC (10 K·min−1, 35–1300 °C); in situ high-temperature PXRD (25–1200 °C); Seebeck coefficient and electrical conductivity (up to 875 °C, He atmosphere); thermal diffusivity (up to 875 °C). Findings: Scandium addition (0.5 wt.%) to Al2CoCrFeNi increases Vickers hardness by 20% due to precipitation hardening.; Electrical conductivity of Al2CoCrFeNi increases by up to 14% with Sc addition.; The maximum dimensionless thermoelectric figure of merit (ZT) of 0.014 is achieved for Al2CoCrFeNi with 0.3 wt.% Sc at 650 °C.; Scandium addition causes grain refinement in Al2CoCrFeNi and transforms the columnar cellular microstructure of AlCoCrCu0.5FeNi into equiaxed non-dendritic grains.; A ternary MgZn2-type intermetallic phase precipitates along grain boundaries in all three alloy systems.; The addition of 3 wt.% Sc stabilizes the CsCl-type phase in Al2CoCrFeNi, shifting the bcc → fcc transformation to approximately 150 °C higher temperatures.; Small punch tests show a decisive increment in brittleness proportional to scandium concentration in Al2CoCrFeNi.. Mechanism: The formation of a hard, stable MgZn2-type ternary intermetallic phase along grain boundaries causes grain refinement and precipitation hardening. Scandium stabilizes the bcc/CsCl phase by affecting the exsolution equilibrium, likely due to the segregation of fcc-stabilizing elements (Ni, Co) into the ternary compound, while Al also segregates into the phase but Cr remains in the matrix.. Limitations: The maximum ZT value of 0.014 is too low to make these materials promising for current thermoelectric applications; the study notes that the synthesis of precipitation-hardened HEAs with binary compounds has proven largely unsuccessful in the past, and the current work focuses on ternary inclusions which are less explored.. Future work: The results could be used as the basis for designing new stable and metastable multicomponent single-phase alloys with improved mechanical properties, and the effect of minor element additions to HEAs should be thoroughly investigated to tackle specific technological needs.. Quote: "The precipitation of a MgZn2-type intermetallic phase along grain boundaries following scandium addition affects all systems differently, but especially enhances the properties of Al2CoCrFeNi."

card: Paper card. Question: Which elemental properties drive phase formation in AlCoCrFeNiTiCu high entropy alloys when inferred solely from chemical concentrations?. System: AlCoCrFeNiTiCu high entropy alloys (7 constituent elements: Al, Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, Ti, Cu). Processing: Trained a feedforward artificial neural network (25-5-3 neurons, Levenberg-Marquardt backpropagation) on 225 experimental samples; generated 8,000 hypothetical samples using Algorithm 1 (min 4 elements, min 10% concentration each); developed primitive rules via Pearson correlation and pruned tree models (max 20 splits); optimized elemental properties using Genetic Algorithm (GA) with Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs) or Euclidean space construction to maximize inter-group distance and minimize intra-group distance.. Test conditions: Dataset of 225 experimental HEA samples; 8,000 generated hypothetical samples; 23 elemental properties considered; GA optimization with mutation probability P_mutation; cost function defined by Equations (1)-(6) with penalty term for correlated variables.. Findings: The neural network achieved an F1-score of 97.4% for FCC phase prediction.; The neural network achieved an F1-score of 95.6% for BCC phase prediction.; The neural network achieved an F1-score of 83.8% for IM phase prediction.; FCC phase formation in the AlCoCrFeNiTiCu family can be predicted with 87% accuracy using only the concentrations of Al and Cu.; Al exhibits a strong negative correlation with FCC formation, while Cu exhibits a strong positive correlation.; Genetic Algorithm optimization with SOMs identified electrical resistivity, molar volume, and electron affinity as the primary phase formation drivers.; Genetic Algorithm optimization with Euclidean space identified density, specific heat, and electron affinity as the primary phase formation drivers.; Electron affinity was the common property identified by both the SOM and Euclidean space methods.. Mechanism: The authors propose that elemental properties responsible for grouping chemical elements into stabilizing (S) and destabilizing (D) sets for specific phases are the drivers of phase formation. They formulate an optimization problem to find the set of properties (e_opt) that maximizes the distance between elements in different groups (S-D) while minimizing the distance between elements in the same group (S-S or D-D) within a topological space (SOM or Euclidean).. Limitations: The network architecture was not optimum, though it yielded satisfactory results. The IM phase prediction had a lower F1-score (83.8%) compared to FCC and BCC. The solution properties are believed to be a proxy to more fundamental properties on the atomic level.. Quote: "FCC phase formation in the AlCoCrFeNiTiCu family of high entropy alloys can be predicted with 87% accuracy by only knowing the concentration of Al and Cu."
W4315853416.title: A machine learning framework for discovering high entropy alloys phase formation drivers

card: Paper card. Question: How can the exploration of the enormous number of High Entropy Alloy (HEA) and Complex Concentrated Alloy (CCA) compositions and their microstructures be accelerated to match the explosion in new alloy bases, and what fundamental data is missing to enable predictive modeling?. System: High entropy alloys (HEAs) and complex concentrated alloys (CCAs), originally defined as blends of 5 or more elements with concentrations between 5 and 35 atom percent, now including systems with as few as 3 principal elements and maximum concentrations higher than 35 atom percent; specific examples mentioned include CoCrFeMnNi, CoCrNi, and Al1.3CoCrCuFeNi.. Findings: The number of HEA systems with 3 to 6 principal elements from a palette of 75 stable elements exceeds 219 million unique systems.; A 5-component system can have 906 different CCA bases if every 10% change in composition gives a distinct base, leading to over 592 billion new CCA bases.; Refractory metal CCAs (RCCAs) exhibit parabolic oxidation kinetics that are two orders of magnitude lower than conventional refractory alloys.; High entropy alloys show exceptional strength, ductility, and fracture toughness at cryogenic temperatures.; The field has explored only seven new alloy families in nearly 15 years, representing a 'linear thinking' approach based on similar atoms.; Current CALPHAD methods cannot predict the presence of ordered B2 intermetallic precipitates in RCCAs because the phase is absent in binary phase diagrams involving refractory metals.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the traditional 'lightly-alloyed-base-element' approach is reaching limits due to a lack of new base elements, whereas HEAs utilize the unexplored central regions of multi-element phase diagrams where all elements are concentrated without a dominant base, creating a vast number of new alloy bases and enabling new physical phenomena such as magnetic hardening and self-healing irradiation resistance.. Limitations: Exploration must accelerate by 6–9 orders of magnitude to match the explosion in new alloy bases; current scientific efforts rely on data collected more than 50 years ago which is limited to single dominant solvent materials; high throughput tests bring a higher degree of uncertainty; and the field has barely scratched the surface by focusing on only seven new alloy families based on similar atoms.. Future work: New high throughput experiments are needed for structural materials; new strategies are needed to navigate the path between composition-dependent and microstructure-dependent properties; acquiring new fundamental data (thermodynamic, phase equilibria, diffusion, etc.) is essential; and the scope of CCA studies must expand to include broader ranges of compositions and uncommon element groupings rather than just equiatomic or near-equiatomic compositions.. Quote: "Exploration must accelerate by 6–9 orders of magnitude to match the explosion in new alloy bases."

card: Paper card. Question: Can binary phase diagrams be used to predict the phase formation (single solid solution, mixed phases, or intermetallics) of high entropy alloys (HEAs) through a phenomenological method combined with machine learning?. System: 614 reported HEAs (Level 3) and 42 newly synthesized complex compositions containing 4 to 7 elements from refractory metals, transition metals, and main group elements (e.g., Al2CoCrCuNi). Processing: Suction casting of master ingots (arc-melted 3 times in high purity argon, 99.7 wt% purity elements) into 3 mm diameter rods; annealing at temperatures > 0.7 Tm for some database entries; phase formation temperature (Tpf) optimized at 0.8 Tm for as-cast alloys. Test conditions: X-Ray Diffraction (XRD) analysis using Cu Kα radiation; Machine Learning classification using Random Forest with 300 trees and 2-10 fold cross-validation on 614 HEAs; validation on 42 new compositions. Findings: The model achieved an overall HEA prediction success rate above 80% and a single-phase HEA prediction rate above 80%.; Validation on 42 randomly selected complex compositions yielded a success rate of 81% (34 out of 42 predicted correctly).; Level 1 (disordered phases) single phase predictions had success rates of 89–90% for as-cast HEAs.; Level 2 (including B2 + SS) overall and B2 + SS phase prediction success rates were near 85%.; Level 3 (including IM+ phases) overall success rate was 80%, with IM+ phase prediction rates of 73–78%.; High accuracy was maintained even with training set percentages as low as 50%.; The optimized phase formation temperature (Tpf) for as-cast HEAs was determined to be 0.8 Tm.. Mechanism: The authors hypothesize that HEA structural stability is encoded within binary phase diagrams; they use phase field percentages at a specific temperature (Tpf) and a phase separation parameter (PSP) to quantify the tendency of constituent binary pairs to form specific phases, which are then combined combinatorially to predict multi-component alloy phases.. Limitations: The study excludes minor phases such as line compounds; mechanically alloyed HEAs are not included because ball milling tends to retain metastable phases; the model's performance slightly abates when annealed HEAs are added to the as-cast set.. Future work: The authors propose including additional physical parameters (e.g., mixing enthalpy) into the ML to improve accuracy, and interacting with other models like CALPHAD where the current model serves as a fast screening tool for in-depth thermodynamic studies.. Quote: "For the first time, a phenomenological method analysing binary phase diagrams to predict HEA phases is presented."

card: Paper card. Question: How can a computationally efficient framework be developed to explore Pareto-optimal compositions and decipher trade-off relationships between strength and ductility in multi-component refractory alloys?. System: Refractory multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) based on Mo, Nb, Ti, Ta, W, Cr, Zr, Hf, and V (specifically MoNbTi and MoNbTiTa systems). Processing: Integration of Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) for elastic constants and misfit volumes, actively learned Moment Tensor Potentials (MTP) for surface and unstable stacking fault energies, and a Virtual Bond Approximation (VBA) analytical model within a Bayesian multi-objective optimization workflow using NSGA-II. Test conditions: Search space constrained to 0.0 ≤ ci ≤ 0.75 for most components (Ti ≤ 0.55); evaluation of properties at ambient conditions via first-principles calculations and analytical models. Findings: The strength of Pareto-optimal MoNbTi alloys ranges from ~50 MPa to ~260 MPa, with ductility index D changing from 1.23 to 1.35.; The addition of Ta to MoNbTi creates a disjoint Pareto set (PFA2) with strength >250 MPa, distinct from the MoNbTi(Ta) region (PFA1).; Surface energy convergence for MoNbTi requires up to 100 atomic layers, whereas typical SQS supercells (~100 atoms) yield errors of 10–20%.; The VBA model reproduces direct CPA+MTP calculations with high accuracy, capturing trends across the entire composition space using only element-specific bandwidths and d-electron counts.; Pearson correlation between predicted ductility index and measured fracture strain is -0.67, correctly ranking alloys at brittle and ductile extremes.; Alloys rich in Ti, Zr, and Nb form a distinct cluster with CRSS 200–400 MPa, while Ta- and W-rich alloys form a separate cluster with higher D values.; The misfit parameter δ and shear modulus G are the primary drivers for CRSS, while surface energy and USF energy govern the ductility index D.. Mechanism: The framework leverages CPA's efficiency for properties insensitive to local relaxations (elastic constants, misfit volumes) and MTP's ability to handle local atomic relaxations for defects (surfaces, USFs). The VBA model extrapolates these trends using universal functions of d-valence and element-specific bandwidths, allowing the identification of optimal trade-offs where strength is tuned via misfit volume and ductility via surface energy.. Limitations: The VBA model cannot replicate strong non-linear effects caused by Fermi-surface transitions (e.g., due to Ta), and the ductility index D does not account for intergranular fracture or grain boundary segregation.. Future work: The methodology can be extended to other mechanical properties like precipitation strengthening, and the VBA model can serve as a surrogate in multi-fidelity optimization frameworks to trigger rare ab initio evaluations.. Quote: "We present a framework to explore Pareto-optimal compositions by integrating advanced ab initio-based techniques into a Bayesian multi-objective optimization workflow."

Paper card. Question: How can a computational framework be constructed to decipher trade-off relationships between intrinsic ductility and yield strength in multi-component alloys, specifically for MoNbTi and MoNbTiTa systems?. System: MoNbTi and MoNbTiTa refractory alloys; elemental compounds and selected binary, three- and four-component alloys. Processing: Integration of Moment Tensor Potentials (MTPs) trained via active learning on DFT data; Multi-objective Bayesian optimization using Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) and NSGAII; Virtual Bond Approximation (VBA) parameterization via CPA calculations; t-SNE dimensionality reduction for visualization. Test conditions: DFT computations with PBE functional, 400 eV energy cutoff, 0.15 Å⁻¹ k-point spacing, 0.08 eV Gaussian smearing; MD simulations at 50K, 150K, and 300K; Yield stress calculations assuming strain rate of 5 ⋅ 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ and reference rate of 10⁴ s⁻¹. Findings: Initial training sets contained 146 and 377 configurations for MoNbTi and MoNbTiTa, respectively, which grew to 381 and 720 configurations after active learning and MD simulations.; Final training set errors for total energies were 6 meV/atom and 19 meV/atom, and for forces 0.099 and 0.104 eV/Å for MoNbTi and MoNbTiTa potentials.; The Bayesian optimization required 36 points for MoNbTi and 143 points for MoNbTiTa (split into two sets of 72 and 71) to converge on the Pareto front.; The Virtual Bond Approximation model was parameterized using CPA calculations for elemental compounds and binary alloys, then adjusted to align with relaxed surface and USF energies of individual elemental compounds.; The ductility index D is defined such that intrinsic ductility is achieved for D < 1 at T = 0K based on the ratio of stress intensity factors for cleavage and dislocation emission.. Mechanism: The framework balances the competition between brittle cleavage (characterized by KIc) and ductile dislocation emission (characterized by KIe) at the crack tip to determine the ductility index. Yield strength is modeled using thermal activation models for solid solution strengthening, while the Virtual Bond Approximation provides a consistent characterization of thermodynamic and elastic properties derived from free energy derivatives.. Limitations: The t-SNE projection provides only an approximate preservation of local structure and distances, leading to an observed patchy pattern. The analytical model for intrinsic ductility is limited to mode I loading. The yield strength model assumes dominating solid solution strengthening and requires subtracting an estimated Hall-Petch contribution from experimental data.. Future work: Integration of recently developed multicomponent magnetic MTPs into the framework to treat magnetic alloys with complex magnetic configurations. Complementing the approach with on-the-fly learning of MLIPs to broaden applicability to systems barely tractable by conventional Kohn-Sham DFT, such as isolated dislocations.. Quote: "Another prospective direction for development is the integration of recently developed multicomponent magnetic MTPs into the presented framework, opening the possibility to treat magnetic alloys with complex magnetic configurations."

card: Paper card. Question: What are the physical origins of the exceptional high-temperature strength and strength retention in refractory body-centered-cubic (BCC) high-entropy alloys (HEAs)?. System: NbTaTiV (nominal Nb25Ta25Ti25V25 at.%) and CrMoNbV (nominal CrMoNbV at.%); search space includes the 10-component Al-Cr-Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-V-W-Zr family.. Processing: Arc-melting of 99.9 wt.% purity elements under argon atmosphere followed by drop-casting into cylindrical rods; NbTaTiV homogenized at 1473 K for 3 days then water-cooled; CrMoNbV tested in the as-cast state.. Test conditions: Uniaxial compression at strain rates of 1 × 10−3 s−1 (NbTaTiV) and 2 × 10−4 s−1 (CrMoNbV); temperatures up to 1173 K; in situ neutron diffraction and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) performed during deformation.. Findings: Neutron diffraction peak broadening analysis yielded q values of -0.6 to -0.4 for NbTaTiV and -2 for CrMoNbV, consistent with edge dislocations and distinct from screw dislocations (+1.9 to +2.1).; Bright-field STEM stereographic analysis of NbTaTiV deformed at 293 K showed 75% (58 of 77) of dislocations were of edge character.; Bright-field STEM stereographic analysis of CrMoNbV deformed at 293 K showed 56% (23 of 41) of dislocations were of edge character.; At 1173 K, edge dislocations remained dominant with 82% (27 of 33) in NbTaTiV and 64% (81 of 127) in CrMoNbV.; The CrMoNbV alloy exhibited the highest reported strength at a homologous temperature of 1173 K.; A computationally guided search over 10^7 BCC HEA compositions identified over 10^6 possible ultra-strong high-temperature alloy compositions.; Theoretical predictions for NbTaTiV strength were lower than experimental values by ~300-500 MPa, attributed to 1.6 at.% O+N interstitial impurities.. Mechanism: In complex HEAs, fluctuations in local solute arrangements create large local variations in potential energy, forcing edge dislocations to adopt a low-energy wavy structure; plastic flow requires thermal activation to overcome large energy barriers created by adjacent high-energy environments, enabling high strength retention at elevated temperatures.. Limitations: The theory does not capture the strength plateau observed at 973–1273 K in many BCC HEAs; neutron pattern quality for CrMoNbV was lower than for NbTaTiV, especially at low plastic strains; the theory assumes a homogeneous average alloy which may not fully capture local complexities.. Future work: Propose fabrication and testing of specific alloys (Mo5W2.5CrZrHf, Mo2.5W2.5CrZrHf, Mo6WCrZrHf, Mo2.5TaWV2.5CrZrHf) with predicted strengths of ~2.5-3 GPa at 1300 K; combine design strategy with detailed thermodynamics and high ductility criteria to discover multi-objective alloys.. Quote: "Here we show, using integrated in-situ neutron-diffraction (ND), high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM), and recent theory, that the high strength and strength retention of a NbTaTiV alloy and a high-strength/low-density CrMoNbV alloy are attributable to edge dislocations."

card: Paper card. Question: How does a novel refractory high entropy alloy (NV1) behave under long-term isothermal oxidation at 1000 °C and 1100 °C, and what is the mechanism governing its oxidation resistance over 200 hours?. System: NV1 alloy (Al, Cr, Mo, Nb, Si, Ta, Ti; designed based on CrMo0.5NbTa0.5TiZr with reduced Ti, removed Zr, and added Al, Si, increased Cr). Processing: Cold crucible levitation melting of high purity elemental raw materials (>99.9 wt%) to cast a 1.1 kg cone-shaped ingot; samples machined by electrical discharge machining and ground to 1200 grit; isothermal oxidation performed in flowing dry air using a thermogravimetric analyser (SETARAM TAG 24-18S) and muffle furnace. Test conditions: Isothermal oxidation at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours in flowing dry air; microstructural characterization performed at intervals of 1, 12, 40, 50, 100, and 200 hours. Findings: At 1000 °C, the mass gain after 200 hours was 6.53 mg/cm2, following an exponential dependence throughout the entire duration.; At 1100 °C, the mass gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm2, which is lower than at 1000 °C, showing three stages of parabolic dependence.; The external oxide layer at both temperatures consisted primarily of a CrTaO4-based oxide with dispersed Al2O3 and Cr2O3.; At 1000 °C, the CrTaO4-based oxide layer was porous with large volume defects due to insufficient kinetics, preventing it from acting as an effective barrier.; At 1100 °C, the CrTaO4-based oxide layer was denser and more continuous, leading to controlled oxidation and reduced weight gain.; TiN particles (size ~1.5 μm) formed preferentially within the Mo-rich dendritic regions at both temperatures, while Al2O3 formed in the internal oxidation depth.; The CrTaO4-based oxide at 1100 °C contained up to 7 at% Al and 2.2 at% less Cr compared to the oxide formed at 1000 °C, indicating non-stoichiometric substitution.. Mechanism: At 1000 °C, insufficient kinetics prevented the formation of a dense, protective CrTaO4 layer, leading to heterogeneous oxidation, volume defects, and exponential weight gain driven by external oxidation and nitridation. At 1100 °C, enhanced diffusion kinetics allowed for the homogeneous growth of a denser, continuous CrTaO4-based layer that acted as a barrier to oxygen and element diffusion, resulting in parabolic weight gain; however, Mo evaporation at the oxide/substrate interface in Stage II temporarily accelerated oxidation before Stage III saw further CrTaO4 formation.. Limitations: The study notes that while CrTaO4-based oxide provided protection, it could not fully prevent the ingestion of oxygen and nitrogen, leading to internal oxidation and nitridation over the long duration.. Future work: The authors propose that the nature of the CrTaO4-based oxide needs to be carefully examined in future studies, and that the influence of nitridation on RHEA properties is an important subject for further investigation.. Quote: "At 1100 °C, mass gain curve showed two parabolic dependences associated with the formation of protective CrTaO4-based oxide layer and the weight gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm2"

card: Paper card. Question: How can machine-learning interatomic potentials be constructed to accurately predict properties of multi-component magnetic alloys by treating magnetic moments as degrees of freedom alongside atomic positions and lattice vectors?. System: bcc Fe–Al alloys with Al concentrations varying from 0 to 50%, including pure bcc-Al. Processing: Training set generation via constrained DFT (cDFT) with hard constraints using ABINIT (6×6×6 k-point mesh, 25 Hartree cutoff, PAW PBE method); 2012 configurations created from 23 parent structures involving geometric relaxation, lattice compression/extension (1%), random atomic displacements (-0.1 to 0.1 Å), and magnetic moment perturbations (up to 15% or 50% deviation); ensemble of five magnetic Moment Tensor Potentials (mMTPs) fitted with 415 parameters (Rmin=2.1 Å, Rcut=4.5 Å, MmaxAl=0.1 μB, MmaxFe=3.0 μB). Test conditions: Verification on 336 additional configurations and fivefold cross-validation on 2328 total configurations; comparison of formation energies, equilibrium lattice parameters, and total magnetic moments against DFT results for various Fe–Al compounds. Findings: The ensemble of mMTPs correctly reproduces the formation energy trend calculated with DFT, which decreases as Al concentration increases.; The maximum error in formation energy prediction is around 20 meV/atom for the Fe8Al8-13682'4'5'7' structure.; The maximum error in equilibrium lattice parameter prediction is about 0.014 Å for the Fe11Al5-12457 structure.; The mMTPs reproduce the anomalous volume-composition dependence in Fe–Al, showing a nearly linear increase up to 18.75% Al, constant values between 18.75% and 31.25%, a decrease between 31.25% and 37.5%, and another increase up to 50%.; The total magnetic moment of the unit cell decreases as the concentration of Al increases, with good agreement between mMTPs and DFT.; A discrepancy was found for the Fe8Al8-12345678 structure where the ensemble of mMTPs predicted zero magnetic moment while DFT predicted 0.7 μB.; Fivefold cross-validation confirmed that fitting and validation errors are close to each other and within the 99% confidence interval.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the anomalous lattice parameter/composition dependence to changes in the magnetic moments of Fe atoms, which are explicitly included as degrees of freedom in the mMTP functional form via constrained DFT training data that allows for non-equilibrium magnetic moments.. Limitations: The ensemble of mMTPs gave a local minimum with zero magnetic moments for the Fe atoms in the Fe8Al8-12345678 structure, whereas DFT predicted a minimum with magnetic moments of 0.7 μB; the force error on the verification set was smaller than the fitting force error, and the stress error on the verification set was two times larger than the fitting stress error.. Future work: The authors plan to develop an active learning algorithm for mMTP to predict material defect properties of other multi-component systems, such as high-entropy alloys, and to train mMTP during molecular dynamics simulations to investigate processes at finite temperature.. Quote: "We propose a machine-learning interatomic potential for multi-component magnetic materials."

card: Paper card. Question: How can computational methods be adapted or developed to address the compositional and configurational complexity of multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) for structural applications, specifically regarding structure generation, interatomic potentials, and machine learning descriptors?. System: Multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) including BCC HfNbTaTiZr, FCC CoCrFeMnNi, CoCrMoxNi, Al0.5CoCrCuFeNi, Ti0.25CrFeNiAlx, TiZrHfNb, TiZrHfAl, RhIrPdPtNiCu, CoFeNi, NbMoTaW, CoCrFeNi, CoCrNi, FeNiCuCoCr, MoNbTaTiV, CuFeNiCrCo, and Al-Co-Cr-Cu-Fe-Ni systems. Processing: Computational design utilizing atomistic structure generation algorithms (Neural evolution structure (NES), Order through informed swapping (OTIS)), Density Functional Theory (DFT), Classical Molecular Dynamics (MD) with various Interatomic Potentials (EAM, Moment tensor potentials (MTP), Low-rank potentials (LRP), Gaussian approximation potential (GAP), Random Fourier feature (RFF), Spectral neighbor analysis potential (SNAP)), and Machine Learning (ML) models (ANNs, decision trees, linear regression) trained on experimental or computational databases. Test conditions: Simulations performed at various scales (up to 40,000+ atoms for NES, hundreds of thousands for OTIS), temperatures including cryogenic and high-temperature (above 600°C), and under conditions of ion irradiation; experimental comparisons made on alloys processed via cold rolling, annealing, and as-cast states. Findings: The Neural evolution structure (NES) generator can create structures with over 40,000 atoms at a reasonable computational overhead of a few hours on 40 processors, significantly reducing complexity compared to SQS.; In BCC MoNbTi, dislocations can glide on higher-order planes, and local slip resistance (LSR) is positively correlated with lattice distortion while anisotropy in LSR is reduced with lattice distortion.; A theoretical model utilizing DFT data (solute misfit volumes, lattice constants, elastic constants, stable stacking fault energies) was developed to predict yield strength in RhIrPdPtNiCu without experimental inputs.; Thermodynamic integration aided by Moment tensor potentials (MTP) offers a four-times speedup compared to DFT-based approaches with less than 1 meV/atom error on high-temperature free energy predictions.; An iterative computational-experimental process in the Al-Co-Cr-Cu-Fe-Ni system identified 42 new candidates, of which 35 had higher hardness than the original dataset, reaching a maximum of 883 HV.; A novel MPEA designed using a database of 370 MPEAs achieved a hardness of 920 HV, outperforming the top original dataset alloy by almost 25%.; In the NbMoTaW refractory HEA system, strengthening was found to be due to the segregation of Nb to the grain boundaries leading to short-range order (SRO).; Stacking fault tetrahedra (SFTs) were identified in CoCrNi medium entropy alloy during irradiation damage, where tetra-vacancy clusters have positive binding energy in CoCrFeMnNi.. Mechanism: The authors argue that unique MPEA properties arise from maximized configurational entropy stabilizing solid solution phases, severe local lattice distortion (LLD) affecting friction stress and yield strength, and element-resolved local lattice distortion (ELLD) driven by charge transfer. Plasticity is governed by compositional inhomogeneities making kink nucleation rate-limiting and creating local slip resistance (LSR) that traps dislocations. Radiation tolerance is enhanced by biased elemental diffusion inducing SRO, higher defect recombination rates, and suppressed damage accumulation. Machine learning models identify correlations between descriptors (e.g., atomic radii, electronegativity, mixing enthalpy) and properties like phase stability and hardness.. Limitations: The text states that SQS generation scales poorly with system size, ab initio methods face size and timescale limitations for dislocation motion, classical potentials miss complex chemical interactions, and current interatomic potentials struggle to model non-equiatomic compositions with micro-alloying. Additionally, experimental databases suffer from discrepancies due to fabrication methods, and ML models often lack interpretability.. Future work: The authors propose better integration of thermodynamic models with ab initio calculations, exploring real-space DFT and efficient sub-space diagonalization, developing reliable interatomic potentials for the periodic table, addressing the disconnect between structure generation algorithms and thermodynamic stability, creating comprehensive computational databases, improving feature selection methods for ML, and enhancing the interpretability of ML models.. Quote: "NES can bring down the computational complexity of structure generation dramatically and has been utilized to create structures with over 40,000 atoms at a reasonable computational overhead (a few hours on 40 processors)."
