card: Paper card. Question: How can the compiled mechanical properties of high entropy alloys (HEAs) and complex concentrated alloys (CCAs) be used to assess their potential as structural materials and guide future development?. System: 370 high entropy alloys (HEAs) and complex concentrated alloys (CCAs), including 3d transition metal, refractory metal (RHEAs and RCCAs), light metal family, and bronzes and brasses HEAs/CCAs families; HEAs defined as alloys with 5 or more principal elements (5-35 at%); CCAs defined as alloys with 3 or more principal components.. Processing: Compilation of data from published reports from 2004 to 2016; density estimated using rule of mixtures (ROM): ρ=∑xiMi/∑xiVi; Young's modulus estimated using ROM for single phase solid solutions only: E=∑xiEi.. Test conditions: Uniaxial loading (tension or compression) at room temperature for 370 alloys; temperature-dependent testing for 27 refractory HEAs (RHEAs).. Findings: The database covers mechanical properties for 370 HEAs and CCAs reported between 2004 and 2016.; For 27 refractory HEAs, yield stress and elongation are provided as a function of testing temperature.; The database includes alloy composition, microstructure type, density, hardness, yield strength, elongation, ultimate strength, and Young's modulus.; Data entries are organized in a tree-like classification with four families and expanded into classes based on principal element combinations.; The database enables users to browse, search, filter, and plot material property maps using performance indices defined by M. F. Ashby.. Mechanism: The authors explain that HEAs are presumably stabilized by the configurational entropy of mixing, while CCAs encompass a broader range of alloys with single-phase or multi-phase microstructures; the database allows for the evaluation of performance indices for lighter, stronger, and stiffer structures.. Limitations: The properties are not equally populated for every alloy due to the lack of literature data.. Future work: The database can be used to represent various property spaces, calculate performance indices, and enable data mining to extract insights and uncover patterns to guide and accelerate the development of HEAs and CCAs.. Quote: "The database covers the main mechanical properties of HEAs and CCAs tested under uniaxial loading from published reports since 2004 until end of 2016."

card: Paper card. Question: How can mechanical properties of refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) and refractory complex concentrated alloys (RCCAs) be systematically compiled and visualized to guide their development as structural materials?. System: 122 refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) and refractory complex concentrated alloys (RCCAs) containing five or more elements with concentrations between 5 and 35 at% (RHEAs) or three or more principal elements with concentrations beyond 35% (RCCAs). Processing: Compilation of data from published reports (2010 to January 2018); metallurgical states include non-equilibrium (as-cast), optimized (homogenization/annealing), hot isostatic pressing (HIP), cold rolling (CR), spark plasma sintering (SPS), and severe plastic deformation (SPD). Test conditions: Uniaxial loading (tension or compression) with strain rates ≤ 10⁻³ s⁻¹; temperature range from −268.8 °C (4.2 K) to 1600 °C (1873 K). Findings: The dataset contains 340 mechanical tests on 122 compositions.; All reported RHEAs and RCCAs crystallize with at least one phase with body centered cubic (BCC) structure.; Yield strength and specific yield strength were visualized as a function of temperature for single-phase and multiphase alloys.; Yield stress was plotted against alloy density at room temperature and 800 °C.; Alloy densities were calculated using the Rule of Mixtures (ROM).; Young's moduli for single-phase alloys were estimated using ROM.. Mechanism: The authors do not propose a physical mechanism for deformation; instead, they argue that the compiled data allows for the visualization of property evolution with temperature and density to identify material solutions for specific applications.. Limitations: The data is limited to studies published through the end of January 2018 and only includes mechanical tests with strain rates less than or equal to 10⁻³ s⁻¹.. Future work: The data compilation can enable machine learning and data analytics methods to extract insights and trends not available from individual studies, thus accelerating the development of these alloys.. Quote: "The comprehensive data compilation provides up-to-date mechanical properties of RHEAs and RCCAs tested under uniaxial loading on the basis of published reports from 2010 through the end of January 2018."

card: Paper card. Question: Can machine learning models accurately predict the elastic constants (C11, C12, C44) of refractory complex concentrated alloys (RCCAs) using a dataset generated from density functional theory (DFT) calculations, and which model performs best?. System: Refractory complex concentrated alloys (RCCAs) with BCC structures containing Cr, Hf, Ta, Ti, Mo, Nb, W, Re, Zr, and V; specific compositions include TiZrVNbMo, TiZrNbMo, TiZrVNb, MoNbTiZr, MoNbTiVZr, NbTiVZr, and NbTaTiV. Processing: Database generation via CALPHAD (Thermo-calc-2019) to identify stable BCC phases, followed by DFT calculations using VASP with GGA-PBE, 500 eV cutoff, and SQS models (8 to 125 atoms); Machine Learning training using Random Forest, Gradient Boosting Regressor (GBR), and XGBoost with 90% training/10% testing split and GridSearchCV hyperparameter tuning. Test conditions: DFT calculations performed at 0 K; ML models validated against 4 unseen experimental and simulation datasets; Performance metrics included R-squared, Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE). Findings: The Gradient Boosting Regressor (GBR) model achieved the highest prediction accuracy with R-squared values of 0.97 for C11, 0.803 for C12, and 0.787 for C44 on the testing dataset.; The Mean Absolute Error (MAE) for the GBR model was below 5 GPa for training data and less than 11 GPa for testing data.; Valence Electron Concentration (VEC) and Melting Temperature (MT) were identified as the top two most influential descriptors for predicting elastic constants.; Higher VEC, MT, and Geometric Parameter (GP) values, combined with lower omega (Ω) values, correlate with higher elastic constants in refractory alloys.; The GBR model predictions for TiZrVNbMo, TiZrNbMo, and TiZrVNb showed good agreement with SQS model calculations, with average error bars smaller than the deviations.; The predicted C11 elastic constant for NbTaTiV matched the experimental value reported by Lee's study very well.; The study utilized a dataset of 370 RCCAs generated from DFT calculations to train the models.. Mechanism: The authors argue that VEC and MT are critical because VEC influences lattice distortion and phase stability (e.g., BCC stability when VEC < 6.87), while higher melting temperatures favor higher elastic constants; the GBR model optimizes bias by iteratively training trees to learn from previous mistakes, avoiding early paralysis and overfitting.. Limitations: The dataset size of 370 instances is relatively small; the ML models do not consider complex phenomena such as lattice defects, dislocations, grain boundaries, slip planes, and plastic deformation; the DFT calculations were performed at 0 K while experiments were at 300 K, causing temperature-related discrepancies; the model cannot predict elastic constants at varying temperatures.. Future work: Future work should focus on creating an ML model that can predict elastic constants at varying temperatures; more high-throughput experimental methods are needed to confirm findings for specific alloys; experimental measurement of lattice distortion is required to gain further knowledge about element contributions; more powerful models should be developed to account for complex phenomena like defects and plastic deformation.. Quote: "The GBR model was found to be most promising in predicting the elastic constant of RCCAs among the three ML models."

card: Paper card. Question: How does valence electron concentration (VEC) control the fracture resistance and deformation mechanisms of cubic-B1 refractory high-entropy carbides (HECs)?. System: Six five-cation rocksalt (B1) HECs: (Ti,Zr,Hf,Nb,Ta)C, (Ti,Zr,Hf,Ta,W)C, (Ti,V,Nb,Ta,W)C, (V,Nb,Ta,Mo,W)C, (V,Ta,Cr,Mo,W)C, and (V,Nb,Cr,Mo,W)C, with VEC ranging from 8.4 to 9.6 e−/f.u.. Processing: High-energy ball milling of binary carbides (Cr3C2, HfC, Mo2C, NbC, TaC, TiC, VC, W2C, ZrC) in argon for 2 hours (30-min intervals with 15-min breaks), followed by spark plasma sintering at 2473 K, 30 MPa uniaxial pressure, 100 K/min heating rate, and 10-min dwell under vacuum.. Test conditions: Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) tensile simulations at 300 K along [001] and [110] directions with 2% strain increments; nanoindentation on polycrystalline samples with loads from 50 to 500 mN and penetration depths up to 1100 nm.. Findings: HECs with VEC ≤ 9.0 e−/f.u. fracture in a brittle manner at theoretical strengths of ≈26 to 27 GPa and elongations of 10 to 14%.; HECs with VEC ≥ 9.4 e−/f.u. yield at ≈8% strain via transformation-induced plasticity rather than fracturing immediately.; High-VEC alloys withstand [001] elongations of 22, 28, and 30% before rupture, compared to 10–14% for low-VEC alloys.; At 50 mN load and 200 nm penetration, low-VEC alloys fracture in ≈20 ± 10% of tests, while high-VEC alloys fracture in only ≈0 to 3%.; At severe conditions (300 mN load, 600 nm penetration), low-VEC alloys fracture in nearly 100% of tests, whereas high-VEC alloys resist fracture in 30 to 60% of tests.; Theoretical tensile toughness (UT) increases superlinearly for VEC > 8.5 e−/f.u., while hardness remains in the range of 27 to 33 GPa for all compositions.; Electron rehybridization in high-VEC alloys facilitates the redistribution of electrons into d-d bonds between next-nearest-neighbor metal atoms during strain.. Mechanism: A high VEC (≳ 9.4 e−/f.u.) enhances fracture resistance by enabling facile rehybridization of electronic metallic states near the Fermi level, which activates transformation plasticity. This allows the material to redistribute electrons into d-d bonds between next-nearest-neighbor metal atoms, modifying bond angles and atomic coordination to dissipate stress and delay rupture, rather than failing via brittle cleavage.. Limitations: The study notes that AIMD simulations use defect-free single-crystal models and high strain rates, yielding ideal upper bounds for strength and elongation that exceed experimental values. Additionally, the presence of native defects (dislocations, grain boundaries), point defects, and stacking faults in real bulk materials causes deviations from the theoretical trends predicted for defect-free crystals.. Future work: The authors propose conducting in-depth transmission electron microscopy to locate stress-induced nanoscale transformations, investigating long-term durability under thermal cycling and oxidation, and performing larger-scale atomistic simulations (nm3 to µm3) using machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) to account for native defects and quantitatively evaluate fracture toughness (KIc).. Quote: "VEC ≳ 9.4 electrons per formula unit enhances alloy fracture resistance due to a facile rehybridization of electronic metallic states, which activates transformation plasticity at the yield point."

card: Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy solid solutions be formed in non-oxide ceramic metal diborides with a hexagonal layered structure, and do they exhibit superior hardness and oxidation resistance compared to their constituent individual diborides?. System: Seven equimolar five-component metal diborides: (Hf0.2Zr0.2Ta0.2Nb0.2Ti0.2)B2, (Hf0.2Zr0.2Ta0.2Mo0.2Ti0.2)B2, (Hf0.2Zr0.2Mo0.2Nb0.2Ti0.2)B2, (Hf0.2Mo0.2Ta0.2Nb0.2Ti0.2)B2, (Mo0.2Zr0.2Ta0.2Nb0.2Ti0.2)B2, (Hf0.2Zr0.2Ta0.2Cr0.2Ti0.2)B2, and (Hf0.2Zr0.2W0.2Mo0.2Ti0.2)B2. Processing: High-energy ball milling (HEBM) for 6 hours in WC media with 60-minute milling/5-minute cooling cycles, followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 2000 °C for 5 minutes under 30 MPa pressure in vacuum (10^-2 Torr). Test conditions: Hardness measured via Vickers indentation at 200 kgf/mm2 with 15s hold time; oxidation resistance assessed via sequential isothermal annealing in flowing dry air at 800–1500 °C for 1 hour per step. Findings: Six of the seven compositions formed a single-phase hexagonal AlB2 structure with greater than 92% of theoretical density.; Aberration-corrected STEM confirmed 2-D high-entropy metal layers separated by rigid boron nets with no detectable layered segregation along the c-axis.; The measured standard deviations of lattice spacings between basal (0001) planes were only ~0.6% of the average c lattice parameter.; Hardness of the high-entropy diborides was generally greater than the average hardness of the five individual constituent metal diborides.; Oxidation resistance was generally better than the average of individual components, with HEB#1 and HEB#7 maintaining shape at 1500 °C while TiB2 pulverized.; Revised Hume-Rothery size-difference factors based on lattice constants (δc) of 3.9% to 5.2% rationalized single-phase formation, whereas the non-single-phase specimen had δc ≈ 6.2%.; Minor secondary oxide phases ((Zr, Hf)O2) were observed in six specimens, and a secondary (Ti1.6W2.4)B4 phase was found in the W-containing specimen.. Mechanism: The formation of high-entropy solid solutions is rationalized by a revised Hume-Rothery size-difference factor calculated from lattice constants rather than atomic radii; the rigid 2-D boron net constrains the metal layers, reducing the effective size mismatch (δa) and allowing entropy stabilization of the disordered solid solution despite larger atomic size differences in the c-direction.. Limitations: The presence of porosity and oxide inclusions resulting from the HEBM procedure adversely affected hardness and oxidation resistance; MoB2 is metastable at room temperature and W2B5 starting powder has limited solubility; the study did not fully optimize microstructure for maximum property performance.. Future work: Further systematic investigation of hardness, oxidation resistance, and other properties is needed, particularly focusing on processing optimization to achieve fully-dense and oxide-free specimens and utilizing the large compositional design space to tailor protective oxide scales.. Quote: "Greater than 92% of the theoretical densities have been generally achieved with largely uniform compositions from nanoscale to microscale."

card: Paper card. Question: Can bulk high-entropy nitrides (HENs) and carbonitrides (HECNs) be synthesized as single-phase materials, and how do configurational entropy and valence electron concentration (VEC) influence their mechanical properties compared to rule-of-mixtures predictions?. System: Five bulk HENs (e.g., (CrMoTaVW)N) and four single-phase bulk HECNs (e.g., (CrMoTaVW)CN) synthesized from equiatomic transition metal precursors; HECN #6 and HECN #3 were multi-phase/segregated.. Processing: Hand-mixing of precursor powders (graphite, mononitrides, monocarbides) with 5 at% graphite; high-energy ball milling (SPEX 8000D, 3 hours, WC media, stearic acid, argon); Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) under vacuum (<30 mtorr) at 100 °C/min ramp, 50 MPa pressure, 1 hour hold; Chromium-containing samples sintered at 1600 °C, others at 2200 °C.. Test conditions: Nanoindentation using 300 mN force with diamond Berkovich indenter (Oliver and Pharr method); 100 indents per sample spaced 30 µm apart; depth ~800 nm; data filtered for outliers (depth >1400 nm and top/bottom 5%); XRD (Cu K-α) and EDS for phase/chemical analysis.. Findings: Synthesized 5 single-phase bulk HENs and 4 single-phase bulk HECNs out of 11 total samples prepared.; Hardness of HENs increased by an average of 22% over the rule-of-mixtures (ROM) average of precursors.; Hardness of HECNs increased by an average of 39% over the ROM average of precursors.; Elastic modulus of HENs increased by an average of 17% over ROM values.; Elastic modulus of HECNs increased by an average of 31% over ROM values.; Hardness shows a negative dependence on valence electron concentration (VEC); increasing VEC decreases hardness.; Configurational entropy positively correlates with the increase in hardness over ROM values (entropic strengthening).; HECN #6 exhibited chemical segregation and two major crystal structures (FCC and hexagonal), while HECN #3 showed minor Nb segregation.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the hardness increase to 'entropic strengthening' caused by compositional randomness, where different element sizes induce local strain that impedes dislocation motion. They propose that carbonitrides have higher configurational entropy than nitrides (1.15R vs 0.8R for equiatomic five-metal systems), leading to greater strengthening. Conversely, increasing VEC enhances metallic bond character, which lowers hardness and modulus by allowing atoms to move to local minima rather than cleaving.. Limitations: The study notes that VEC is an oversimplification for quantifying electronic structure, as mononitrides with equal VEC can have vastly different hardness. Additionally, the Entropy Forming Ability (EFA) descriptor indicates that some compositions (like HECN #3) may require more energetic input to achieve homogeneity. The authors also state they have not determined if the materials are truly entropy-stabilized, as enthalpic contributions and mutual solubility exist.. Future work: The authors suggest that purposeful design of configurational entropy and VEC can tune mechanical properties and high-temperature phase stability. They propose that universal adoption of the sublattice model for calculating configurational entropy will bolster the understanding and design of entropy-related properties in high-entropy ceramics.. Quote: "The hardness of HENs and HECNs increased by an average of 22% and 39%, respectively, over the rule-of-mixtures average of their monocarbide and mononitride precursors."

card: Paper card. Question: How can the large compositional space of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloys be mapped to identify optimal elemental fractions that simultaneously maximize kinetic energy dissipation while minimizing projectile penetration depth and residual velocity under high-velocity impact?. System: AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloys (HEAs) with atomic fractions: Fe [15%, 25%], Ni [15%, 25%], Co [15%, 25%], Cr [15%, 25%], Al [0–40%]. Processing: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations using LAMMPS with EAM/alloy force-field for HEA and Lennard-Jones for Au-HEA interface; 0.1 fs time-step; NPT ensemble equilibration at 300 K and 0 bar for 10 ps; NVE ensemble for impact; Gaussian Process (GP) machine learning model with Matern 2.5 kernel (scale 5.5) trained on 64 quasi-random Sobol samples; Multi-objective genetic algorithm (MOGA) with population size 100, crossover rate 0.8, adaptive mutation.. Test conditions: Cylindrical gold projectiles (radius 28 Å, height 78 Å) impacting cylindrical AlCoCrFeNi target plates (radius 215 Å, thickness 60.52 Å) at impact velocities (Vi) ranging from 400 m/s to 1100 m/s; strain rates spanning 10⁻¹ to >10⁴ s⁻¹.. Findings: Prediction error of the Gaussian Process models remains within ±10% for kinetic energy dissipation (ΔKE), penetration depth (δ), and residual velocity (Vr).; Increasing impact velocity from 400 to 1100 m/s results in a 49.4% increase in ΔKE, 35.3% increase in penetration depth (δ), and 12.46% increase in residual velocity (Vr).; Increasing atomic fractions of Fe, Co, and Cr leads to increased kinetic energy dissipation and penetration depth, whereas increasing Ni and Al concentrations decreases both.; The configuration with 25% Al and 0% Ni (Al25(FeCrCo)75Ni0) exhibits the highest transverse displacement (penetration depth) and highest kinetic energy dissipation, along with the lowest residual velocity.; The FCC to HCP lattice transition involves approximately 1% of atoms in equiatomic AlCoCrFeNi HEA, compared to 3.73% (29,979 atoms) in the Al25(FeCrCo)75Ni0 HEA.; The optimal solution from multi-objective genetic algorithm maximizes ΔKE while minimizing δ and Vr, with direct MD validation showing perfect agreement with ML-MOGA predictions.; Residual velocity shows a sharp decline specifically with increasing Al concentration, unlike other elements which show mild or positive correlations.. Mechanism: Increased Al concentration and decreased Ni concentration enhance plastic deformation of the target plate, leading to greater transverse displacement (penetration depth) and higher kinetic energy dissipation; the FCC to HCP structural transition is more extensive in high-Al/low-Ni alloys, contributing to higher energy dissipation.. Limitations: The study is limited to the AlCoCrFeNi system and does not experimentally validate the results; the computational framework relies on the accuracy of the EAM and Lennard-Jones force-fields and the assumption of single-phase FCC structure for the modeled compositions.. Future work: The proposed generic computational framework can be extended to other HEA systems and various multi-physical property demands with conflicting objectives and inherent simulation variabilities.. Quote: "The data-driven analysis reveals that a lower concentration of Ni with a higher concentration of Al leads to higher dissipation of kinetic energy and lower residual velocity, but with higher penetration depth of the projectile."

card: Paper card. Question: What is the mechanical behavior and resistance to shear localization of the single-phase fcc Al0.3CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy under high strain-rate dynamic loading?. System: Al0.3CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy (single phase fcc). Processing: Vacuum-induction melting to cast a plate (~127 mm × 305 mm × 19 mm), followed by hot-isostatic-pressing (HIP) at 1,204 °C and 103 MPa for 4 hours, homogenization at 1,200 °C for 2 hours, and water quench.. Test conditions: Quasi-static compression (strain rate 10−4 s−1), dynamic compression using Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar (strain rates up to 1800 s−1 and 104 s−1), and forced shear localization using hat-shaped specimens at high strain rates.. Findings: Yield stress increases from 216 MPa to 503 MPa as strain rate increases from 10−4 s−1 to 1.8 × 102 s−1.; Strain-rate sensitivity (m) is approximately 0.053, which is double that of coarse-grained pure aluminum (0.028).; The strain hardening rate of the alloy exceeds 1000 MPa, significantly higher than that of coarse-grained pure aluminum.; No adiabatic shear band was observed in hat-shaped samples subjected to an imposed shear strain of ~1.1.; At a strain rate of 104 s−1 and true strain of 0.5, the calculated temperature rise is only 109 K (to 402 K).; Mechanical twins with a ~36% area fraction and ~2.4 μm average thickness were observed in the deformed region.; Dynamic recrystallization was absent in the forced shear region, indicating the material continued to harden rather than soften.. Mechanism: The authors propose that the combination of solid solution hardening, forest dislocation hardening, and mechanical twinning creates an excellent work hardening ability that suppresses shear localization. This high strain hardening ability, coupled with high strain-rate sensitivity and modest thermal softening, prevents the thermal softening from overcoming strain hardening, thereby inhibiting the formation of adiabatic shear bands.. Limitations: The authors state that adiabatic shear localization of this alloy can only be activated by higher strains and temperatures than those imposed by their experiments.. Quote: "The combination of multiple strengthening mechanisms such as solid solution hardening, forest dislocation hardening, as well as mechanical twinning leads to a high work hardening rate"

card: Paper card. Question: Why does the Mn-free HEA (CrFeCoNi) exhibit higher ballistic resistance than the Mn-containing Cantor alloy (CrMnFeCoNi), and what are the underlying deformation mechanisms during high-speed impact?. System: CrMnFeCoNi (Cantor alloy) and CrFeCoNi (Mn-free companion). Processing: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations using LAMMPS with 2NN MEAM potential; ballistic impact simulated by a 3 nm iron rigid sphere at 25 nm/ps; uniaxial tension at strain rates of 5 × 10^7, 5 × 10^8, and 5 × 10^9 s^-1; temperatures of 70 K, 300 K, and 1000 K.. Test conditions: Room temperature (300 K) for ballistic impact; high strain rates (10^7 to 10^9 s^-1); plate thicknesses of 2.29 nm and 6.04 nm; bullet speed 25 nm/ps.. Findings: The Mn-free HEA (CrFeCoNi) blocked the high-speed sphere at a smaller penetration depth (2 ps) compared to the Mn-containing HEA (2.5 ps).; The Mn-free HEA exhibited stronger interatomic bonding with a cohesive energy of -4.25 eV per atom, versus -4.01 eV per atom for the Mn-containing alloy.; Higher strain rates induced more active dislocations, significantly enhancing the strain hardening and toughness of the Mn-free HEA.; Dislocation tangling occurred earlier and more easily in the Mn-containing HEA due to Mn's larger atomic radius causing lattice distortion.; The Mn-containing HEA showed more amorphization and structural damage throughout the plate, while the Mn-free HEA maintained better structural integrity.; Deformation twinning was not a dominant factor at room temperature; planar-slip dislocations played the predominant role in plastic deformation.; The Mn-free HEA had a lower stacking fault energy (more negative) than the Mn-containing HEA, favoring the dissociation of full dislocations into partial dislocations.. Mechanism: The superior ballistic resistance of CrFeCoNi is attributed to its stronger interatomic bonding (due to Mn's lower electron work function in CrMnFeCoNi) and higher dislocation density generated at high strain rates. In CrFeCoNi, energy is absorbed by activating dislocations and strain hardening, whereas in CrMnFeCoNi, weaker bonding and easier dislocation tangling lead to bond breaking, amorphization, and severe structural damage.. Limitations: The MD simulation dimensions (nanometers) are significantly smaller than real-world ballistic tests (millimeters to centimeters), which may limit the space for dislocation development, though the authors argue this does not affect the calculated influence of Mn on bonding strength.. Future work: Sufficient attention needs to be given to the modification of the atomic bonding strength in addition to the plastic deformation mechanism when designing armor and energy-absorption HEAs and related materials.. Quote: "Stronger atomic bonding and higher dislocation densities make the CrFeCoNi easier to be strain hardened with elevated toughness to resist high-speed deformation"

card: Paper card. Question: How do crystal structure, alloy composition, grain size, and twin boundary distance influence the mechanical characteristics, deformation mechanisms, and microstructure evolution of AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys during nanoimprinting?. System: AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys (specifically Al0.3, Al0.4, Al0.5, and Al0.7 compositions in FCC structure). Processing: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulation using LAMMPS with EAM potential for interatomic interactions and Lennard-Jones potential for punch-sample interaction; punch moved at 25 m/s to 30 Å penetration depth at 300 K. Test conditions: Temperature: 300 K; Loading speed: 25 m/s; Penetration depth: 30 Å; Time step: 1.0 fs; Crystal structures: monocrystalline, polycrystalline, nano-twinned polycrystalline; Grain sizes: 51.43–80.03 Å; Twin boundary distances: 6.61–30.42 Å. Findings: Highest imprinting forces were 830.20 nN (polycrystalline), 866.92 nN (NT-polycrystalline), and 930.38 nN (monocrystalline).; Maximum imprinting force increased with Al content: 736.20 nN (Al0.3), 778.04 nN (Al0.4), 830.20 nN (Al0.5), and 877.67 nN (Al0.7).; Reverse Hall–Petch relation observed for polycrystalline structure where smaller grain sizes (51.43 Å) resulted in lower loading forces (730.07 nN) compared to larger grains (80.03 Å, 879.45 nN).; Hall–Petch and reverse Hall–Petch relations found for NT-polycrystalline: peak force 866.92 nN at 13.16 Å TB distance, dropping to 679.90 nN at 6.61 Å.; Shear strain and local stress concentrated around the punch and on grain/twin boundaries (GBs/TBs).; Elastic recovery ratio was insensitive to alloy composition and grain size changes.; Formability of the pattern was higher with a decrease in twin boundary (TB) distance.. Mechanism: The authors argue that grain boundaries (GBs) and twin boundaries (TBs) inhibit dislocation movement and plastic deformation. In polycrystalline structures, the slide and twist of GBs control deformation, while in NT-polycrystalline structures, TB migration and the interaction of dislocations with TBs are dominant. The presence of TBs enhances grain stability and strength up to a critical distance, after which excessive TBs lead to softening (reverse Hall–Petch).. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study.. Future work: The text does not explicitly state future work proposed by the authors.. Quote: "The reverse Hall–Petch relation found for the polycrystalline structure, while the Hall–Petch and reverse Hall–Petch relations are discovered in the NT-polycrystalline, which is due to the interactions between the dislocations and grain/twin boundaries (GBs/TBs)."
